Atopic Eczema — A Disrupted Skin Barrier

Source-backed clinical infographic on atopic dermatitis, barrier dysfunction, variable symptoms, assessment, management and infection warning signs.

Research behind the infographic

  • Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, often starting in childhood but possible at any age; it is not contagious. [1] [2]
  • Barrier changes allow moisture to escape and expose the skin immune system to the environment; genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause. [1]
  • Skin has a protective outer layer; a schematic intact-versus-disrupted surface comparison illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin. [1]
  • Inflammation can trigger itch; scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation and increases bacterial infection risk. [1] [3]
  • Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin; scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid. [1] [2]
  • Eczema appearance varies with skin tone: it can appear red, purple, grey or lighter or darker than surrounding skin; inflammation may leave color changes. [1] [2]
  • Common sites include elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have facial eczema. Distribution varies by age and can occur elsewhere. [1] [2]
  • Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement; itch can disturb sleep. [1] [2]
  • Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with increased likelihood, not proof of one cause. [1] [2]
  • Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms; triggers vary by person. [1] [2] [3]
  • Diagnosis involves clinical skin examination and medical, family and trigger history; clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes. [3]
  • Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps retain water and supports the skin barrier; gentle unscented or non-soap cleansing and lukewarm water can help. [2] [3]
  • Avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce scratching damage; do not change diet unless advised by a clinician. [2] [3]
  • Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines may be considered by clinicians depending on severity, age and response, not as universal treatments. [2] [3]
  • Treatment can control symptoms but there is currently no cure; seek care for symptoms or treatments that are not helping. [1] [2]
  • Painful warm swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking/crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum and warrant urgent medical advice. [2]
  • Emollients transferred onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make fabrics catch fire more easily; avoid smoking and naked flames. [2]

Sources

  1. Atopic Dermatitis: Overview, Symptoms and Causes — NIAMS, National Institutes of Health
  2. Atopic eczema — NHS
  3. Atopic Dermatitis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take — NIAMS, National Institutes of Health

Cataract — Light Through a Clouded Lens

Source-backed medical infographic explaining cataract anatomy, symptoms, risk factors, diagnosis, early functional aids, surgery and separate retinal-detachment warnings.

Research behind the infographic

  • A cataract is clouding of the natural lens; the normally clear lens bends incoming light to help vision. [1] [2]
  • The cornea, iris and lens are front-of-eye structures; the pupil is widened by dilation, and the retina and optic nerve are examined at the back of the eye. [2]
  • The retina is the light-sensitive tissue layer at the back of the eye. [3]
  • Age-related changes cause lens proteins to break down and clump, creating cloudy areas; most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates. [1] [2]
  • Cataracts can affect one or both eyes but do not spread between eyes. [1]
  • Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night and ghosted or double images in the affected eye can occur; symptoms can also reflect other eye problems. [1] [2]
  • Older age, smoking, diabetes, sun exposure, steroid use, family history and previous eye injury are cataract risk factors; these do not establish an individual diagnosis. [1] [2]
  • Evaluation includes visual acuity or refraction, slit-lamp examination of front-of-eye structures, and a dilated examination to check the eye including retina and optic nerve. [1] [2]
  • For mild symptoms, updated glasses, brighter reading light and magnification can help function but do not remove the cataract. [1] [2]
  • Only surgery removes a cataract; the cloudy natural lens is removed and replaced by an artificial intraocular lens (IOL). [1] [2]
  • Surgery is considered when cataracts interfere with everyday activities; immediate surgery is not always needed, and benefits and risks should be discussed with an ophthalmologist. [1] [2]
  • UV-protective sunglasses and a brimmed hat, stopping smoking and protective eyewear can help reduce avoidable eye risks; these measures do not guarantee cataract prevention. [1] [2]
  • Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow across vision can signal retinal detachment rather than gradual cataract change; seek an eye doctor or emergency room immediately. [3]

Sources

  1. Cataracts — National Eye Institute
  2. What Are Cataracts? — American Academy of Ophthalmology
  3. Retinal Detachment — National Eye Institute

Gallstones — When Bile Flow Is Blocked

Detailed biliary anatomy and eight panels explaining stone formation, blockage, clinical features, risk, assessment, management and warning signs.

Research behind the infographic

  • The pear-shaped gallbladder lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen and stores bile produced by the liver. [1]
  • Bile passes through hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum; the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum. [1]
  • Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food. [1]
  • Gallstones are hard pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder; cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green and pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin. [1]
  • Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin, insufficient bile salts, or the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently; the reasons for bile changes are not fully understood. [2]
  • Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms; asymptomatic gallbladder stones usually need no treatment. [1] [2] [3] [4]
  • A stone obstructing a bile duct can cause bile buildup and biliary colic; attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends. [2]
  • Pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen, last several hours, and accompany nausea or vomiting; attacks often follow heavy meals. [2] [4]
  • Persistent blockage can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection, or gallstone pancreatitis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes. [1] [2] [4]
  • Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity, rapid weight loss, and in women; risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis. [1] [4]
  • Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests; similar symptoms may have other causes requiring clinical assessment. [2] [4]
  • The main treatment for symptomatic gallstones is gallbladder removal, often laparoscopic; ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances. [3] [4]
  • After gallbladder removal, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum rather than being stored in a gallbladder. [3]
  • Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce gallstone risk; they do not guarantee prevention or dissolve existing stones. [1] [3] [4]
  • Seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting; dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications. [2] [4]

  2. Symptoms & Causes of Gallstones — NIDDK
  3. Treatment for Gallstones — NIDDK
  4. Gallstones — NHS

Iron-Deficiency Anemia — Oxygen Delivery Under Strain

Eight-panel anatomical plate explaining iron-deficiency anemia, blood-cell morphology, sources of iron loss, intake and absorption, variable symptoms, CBC versus ferritin, cause-specific care, nutrition support, and possible untreated complications.

Research behind the infographic

  • Iron deficiency can impair production of healthy red blood cells; low hemoglobin in anemia reduces oxygen carriage from lungs to other organs. [1] [2]
  • Iron-deficiency anemia can show small red blood cells with pale centers on a blood smear; low mean cellular volume is a common laboratory finding. [2]
  • Blood loss removes iron; heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are causes requiring evaluation. [1] [2]
  • Low intake of iron-containing foods can contribute; celiac disease and stomach or intestinal surgery can impair iron absorption. [1] [2]
  • Mild or moderate iron-deficiency anemia may have no symptoms; more serious disease can cause fatigue, dizziness, pale skin, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, or chest pain. [1]
  • Evaluation includes medical and diet history, a complete blood count with hemoglobin and cell size, ferritin, and other iron studies; further testing depends on suspected cause. [1] [2]
  • Low ferritin indicates reduced iron stores; iron deficiency can occur without anemia, so hemoglobin alone does not establish iron-store status. [2]
  • Treatment depends on cause and severity; clinician-guided oral iron is common, and intravenous iron may be used for poor absorption, intolerance, severe deficiency, or chronic blood loss. [1] [2]
  • Oral iron may cause upset stomach or constipation; significant symptoms should be discussed with the treating clinician. [1] [2]
  • Iron replacement must be paired with finding and treating the underlying cause; transfusion is reserved for selected severe cases and does not completely correct iron deficiency. [2]
  • Beans, tofu, lean red meat, fortified cereals, and dark leafy greens provide iron; vitamin-C-rich foods such as oranges can support absorption. [1]
  • Treating blood loss or absorption problems may help prevent iron-deficiency anemia; diet supports iron intake but is not a universal substitute for treatment. [1] [2]
  • Untreated iron-deficiency anemia may lead to heart problems, pregnancy complications, or developmental delays in children. [1]

Sources

  1. Anemia — Iron-Deficiency Anemia — National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
  2. Iron-Deficiency Anemia — American Society of Hematology

Arachnophobia — The Spider at the Curtain Fold

Source-backed educational infographic distinguishing arachnophobia, anticipation and physical symptoms from actual danger, with avoidance and evidence-based professional support.

Research behind the infographic

  • Arachnophobia is fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia. [1] [3]
  • Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger. [1]
  • Seeing the feared object can cause immediate anxiety; anticipation and even thinking about it can also cause anxiety. [1] [3]
  • Some people with arachnophobia avoid touching a spider; some cannot look at a spider picture. [3]
  • Physical symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea; experiences vary. [2]
  • People may actively avoid feared objects and organise life around avoidance, limiting daily activities. [1] [3]
  • A repeated encounter can provoke anxiety again; avoidance and intense anxiety are common features, not proof of actual danger. [1] [3]
  • It is not always clear why a phobia develops; frightening experiences and learned fear can be involved. [1] [2]
  • CBT is an effective treatment; exposure therapy is a CBT method particularly effective for phobias. [1]
  • Exposure treatment can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object; plans differ and a specialist can help. [3]
  • Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms, and triggering images may be distressing. [2]
  • Seek a primary care or qualified mental health professional when symptoms interfere with life. [1] [2] [3]

Sources

  1. Phobias and Phobia-Related Disorders — National Institute of Mental Health
  2. Phobias — NHS

Dentophobia — Waiting Beside the Dental Chair

Source-backed educational dentophobia plate distinguishing fear, sensory triggers, variable physical symptoms, care avoidance, realistic pain concerns and tailored support.

Research behind the infographic

  • Dental anxiety can occur before a visit; severe persistent dental fear can lead to avoidance. Ordinary nervousness does not itself establish a phobia. [3]
  • Dental fear can be associated with feared pain, previous difficult experiences, unfamiliar procedures, or a perceived lack of control. [1] [3]
  • The sights of dental instruments, drilling sounds and vibrations, clinical smells, and the reclined dental-chair position can trigger anxiety for some people. [3]
  • Uncertainty about what will happen can contribute to anxiety; asking questions about the procedure can help reduce fear of the unknown. [1] [3]
  • Possible anxiety responses include a noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension and sweaty palms; symptoms vary. [2] [3]
  • Avoiding dental care can increase the risk of dental problems and make later visits more difficult, reinforcing fear; this is a possible cycle, not an inevitable outcome. [1] [3]
  • Fear can concern perceived danger; pain concerns should not be dismissed. Patients should discuss pain management and tell the dentist if pain occurs even with local anesthetic. [1] [3]
  • Tell the dental team about anxiety and previous experiences; ask what will happen and agree on a raised-hand signal to pause. [1]
  • Headphones for bothersome drilling sounds, a handheld stress ball, slow breathing and relaxing tense muscles can help manage dental anxiety. [1]
  • CBT and professionally guided exposure-based approaches can help with dental phobia; management should be tailored to the person and clinical situation. [2] [3]
  • Seek professional help when phobia symptoms affect life; a dentist and mental-health professional may work together on care. [2] [3]

Sources

  1. Anxiety — American Dental Association
  2. Phobias — NHS
  3. Strategies to manage patients with dental anxiety and dental phobia: literature review — Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dentistry

Aquaphobia — At the Quiet Pool Edge

Source-backed educational plate distinguishing intense fear of water from genuine aquatic hazards, with variable symptoms and evidence-based support.

Research behind the infographic

  • Aquaphobia is intense fear of water or drowning; specific phobia involves fear out of proportion to the actual danger in a particular situation. [1] [4]
  • Water exposure, thoughts of water, and reluctance to enter water or immerse the face or body can accompany fear of water; individual experiences vary. [1] [4]
  • Unfamiliar aquatic perceptive cues can accompany anxiety; a small exploratory study described concerns about depth, locating the surface, and finding solid support. These are illustrative concerns, not universal symptoms or a safety assessment. [4]
  • Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea, and dizziness; not everyone has every symptom. [2]
  • Anticipation or encountering a feared situation can bring intense anxiety and active avoidance; phobias may interfere with daily life. The sequence illustrates repeated encounters and avoidance, not a universal causal diagnosis. [1] [2]
  • Fear of water can interfere with learning to swim and can persist into adulthood. [4]
  • Natural water may have currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, and limited visibility; genuine hazards should not be dismissed as anxiety. [3]
  • Swimming lessons can reduce drowning risk; swimming with a buddy and choosing lifeguarded sites when possible remain important precautions. [3]
  • Life jackets reduce drowning risk while boating and can help weaker swimmers around natural water and pools; inflatable or foam toys are not safety devices. [3]
  • CBT is an established treatment for phobias, and exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method; healthcare professionals can help determine next steps. No water-entry treatment protocol is provided. [1]
  • Talk to a healthcare professional if symptoms affect life. Breathing exercises and talking to someone trusted can help manage symptoms; anxiety management does not replace water safety. [1] [2] [3]
  • The hero and dry-land help vignettes are illustrative, not a diagnosis or instruction to enter water. [1] [3]

Sources

  1. Phobias and Phobia-Related Disorders — National Institute of Mental Health
  2. Phobias — NHS
  3. Preventing Drowning — Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
  4. Reducing fear of water and aquaphobia through 360 degree video use? — Frontiers in Education

Pyrophobia — The Candle Behind Glass

Eight-panel fire-fear educational plate with a glass-partition candle hero, symptom map, anticipation and avoidance sequence, real safety comparison, CBT and support.

Research behind the infographic

  • Specific phobias involve intense fear out of proportion to actual danger; this plate applies that framework to fear of fire. [1]
  • Anticipating a feared object or situation can cause excessive worry; encountering it can cause immediate intense anxiety. [1]
  • People may actively avoid feared objects and situations or endure them with intense anxiety. [1]
  • Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea. [2]
  • Avoidance can restrict activities; exposure-based CBT helps people engage in activities and situations they have avoided. [1]
  • CBT teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias. [1]
  • Relaxation exercises may accompany exposure therapy; breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms. [1] [2]
  • Seek a primary care provider when symptoms affect life; a provider can refer to a qualified mental health professional. [1] [2]
  • Open flames are dangerous if candles tip over or are too close to combustible objects; ordinary fire precautions remain necessary. [3]
  • Consider battery-operated flameless candles; lit candles need stable holders, at least 12 inches from anything that burns, and should be extinguished when leaving the room or before bed. [3]
  • Use flashlights rather than candles during a power outage. [3]

Sources

  1. Phobias and Phobia-Related Disorders — National Institute of Mental Health
  2. Phobias — NHS
  3. Candle Fire Safety — U.S. Fire Administration

Aurora — From Magnetosphere to Photon

An eight-panel source-backed educational plate tracing magnetospheric energy transfer, electron precipitation, excitation, emission color, collision quenching and auroral geometry.

Research behind the infographic

  • Solar wind transfers energy into Earth’s magnetosphere; solar wind pressure stretches a magnetotail away from the Sun. [1] [2]
  • Oppositely directed solar-wind and terrestrial magnetic fields favor energy transfer through magnetic reconnection. [1] [2]
  • Auroral electrons are accelerated within the magnetosphere; nighttime auroral electrons can come from the magnetotail, rather than arriving directly as solar-wind electrons. [2]
  • Accelerated electrons follow magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere near magnetic poles. [1] [2]
  • Collisions transfer energy from electrons to atmospheric atoms and molecules, exciting them; relaxation releases photons. [1] [2]
  • Excited atomic oxygen produces green and red light; nitrogen can produce blue and pink-purple light. [1] [2]
  • Red oxygen emission is favored higher in the thinner atmosphere; green oxygen emission and pink-purple nitrogen lower borders can occur below it; these are tendencies, not rigid altitude boundaries. [1] [2]
  • The excited oxygen state producing red light is longer lived than the green-emitting state; collisions can quench red emission in denser lower air before a photon is emitted. [2]
  • Auroral emissions form ovals around magnetic poles, not a single spot over the geographic pole. [2]
  • Quiet displays can be simple arcs; greater geomagnetic activity can yield brighter multiple arcs, rays, waves and curls, and expand the oval toward lower latitudes. [2]
  • Cameras can detect auroral colors too dim for human eyes; faint auroras may look pale to a person because night vision favors brightness over color. [1] [2]

Sources

  1. Auroras — NASA
  2. Aurora Tutorial — NOAA / NWS Space Weather Prediction Center

Burying Beetle — A Nursery Beneath the Soil

Species-specific carrion preparation, social immunity and facultative parental provisioning in a burying beetle.

Research behind the infographic

  • Nicrophorus vespilloides is a real burying beetle in the genus Nicrophorus, family Silphidae. [1] [3]
  • The adult specimen has a black head and pronotum, black clubbed antennae, six jointed legs, and orange transverse markings on dark, shortened elytra with the abdominal tip exposed; the reference photo supplies diagnostic visual anatomy. [3]
  • N. vespilloides occurs in woodland populations west of Cambridge, England; the illustrated leaf litter and soil are a representative woodland context, not a full-range map. [4]
  • Adults locate small vertebrate carrion, which serves as the breeding resource and food for offspring; adults use flight in locating carrion. [1] [5]
  • Parents remove fur or feathers, roll the flesh into a ball and bury the prepared carcass in an underground chamber. [1]
  • Parents smear the carcass with exudates that inhibit microbial growth; this is social immunity, not complete sterilization. [2]
  • Lysozymes are antimicrobial enzymes implicated in social immunity; female anal-exudate antimicrobial properties correlate with expression of a particular lysozyme gene. No specific molecular cutting reaction is illustrated. [2]
  • After hatching, larvae feed on the prepared carcass and can also receive regurgitated meat from parents; mouth-to-mouth feeding is depicted as provisioning, not attack. [1]
  • Biparental and single-parent care occur in this species; the illustrated pair is one possible family arrangement, not an obligation. [1] [5]
  • Larvae disperse from the carrion for pupation and later emerge as adults; the life-history strip is schematic, not to scale and gives no fixed timing or brood size. [1] [5]
  • Carrion is a scarce resource and beetles compete over it; mandibles are used in contests, with larger individuals often advantaged, not guaranteed winners. [4] [5]
  • The beetles transform vertebrate carrion into food for growing offspring, an ecological carrion-use relationship; no broader quantified recycling benefit is claimed. [1] [5]

Coccolithophores — Building Ocean Chalk

Eight-panel source-backed educational plate explaining intracellular coccolith formation, overlapping calcite architecture and marine carbonate pathways.

Research behind the infographic

  • Noelaerhabdaceae coccoliths have multiple calcite crystal segments radially distributed around a central grid; they have proximal and distal shields. [2]
  • Completed coccoliths are extruded from the cell to form an overlapping external covering called a coccosphere. [2]
  • Additional coccoliths enter surrounding seawater when cells multiply, die or produce excess plates. [1]

  • Coccolith size and mass vary among species and even within a single coccosphere; the study used three-dimensional X-ray imaging to separate plates and measure geometry. [2]

Tsunami — The Shoaling Water Column

Source-backed mechanism plate on tsunami shoaling and coastal water-column change.

Research behind the infographic

  • Tsunamis propagate through the entire water depth, unlike wind waves whose motion is concentrated near the surface. [1]
  • In deep ocean water, a tsunami has a long wavelength and often small surface height; it may be barely noticeable. [1] [2]
  • Tsunami propagation speed depends on water depth: deeper water permits faster propagation; shallower water slows it. [1] [2]
  • For a long wave, propagation speed c is approximated by sqrt(g h), where g is gravitational acceleration and h water depth. [1]
  • As a tsunami enters shallower water, its wavelength decreases. [1] [2]
  • Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength; slowing propagation does not itself change frequency, so wavelength becomes shorter. [2]
  • Shoaling is the increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water; tsunami waves can grow much taller near the coast. [1] [2]
  • Currents intensify as tsunamis approach shallow coastal water. [1]
  • Even after shoaling, tsunami wavelengths remain relatively long; water can continue flowing inland for many minutes. [2]
  • Run-up refers to the maximum height reached inland above normal sea level, distinct from horizontal inundation extent. [2]

Sources

  1. Tsunami Propagation — NOAA
  2. Tsunami shoaling — University of Waikato — Science Learning Hub

  • Avoiding sleep-related reminders may occur in trauma-related fear; reliance on avoidance can make trauma symptoms worse and impede recovery. [3] [4]
  • Fear can be disproportionate to a threat; the intensity of a fear response is not itself evidence of current danger. Real sleep symptoms warrant individual assessment. [2] [3]
  • Talking therapies including CBT can help phobias; seek a health professional when symptoms affect daily life. [2]
  • CBT-I reduced fear of sleep in a trial of adults with both PTSD and insomnia; that finding is specific to that studied group, not a universal promise. [3]
  • Fear of sleep is not identical to insomnia; in the studied PTSD sample it related to nightmares and hypervigilance rather than classic insomnia symptoms. [3]

Thanatophobia — Fear of Death

Artwork-led educational chart explaining the established name, death-related reminders, anxiety symptoms, avoidance and professional support without presenting ordinary mortality awareness as illness.

Research behind the infographic

  • Thanatophobia is an established term for fear of death; the displayed definition is Fear of death. [1]
  • Death anxiety is studied across multiple mental health conditions; the term is not being presented as a separate diagnosis in this educational chart. [2] [4]
  • Awareness of mortality is common; distress and disruption of daily life warrant assessment rather than assuming all death-related worry is illness. [4] [3]
  • Death-related conversations and news can act as reminders that provoke death anxiety; thoughts of one’s own death can be feared. [4]
  • Phobic anxiety may include palpitations, dizziness and trembling; symptoms differ between people. [3]
  • Avoidance of death-related reminders can be an unhelpful coping behavior maintaining death anxiety; short-term relief should not be equated with lasting recovery. [2] [4]
  • Perceived threat can exceed the current situation: a reminder or frightening thought is not itself evidence of imminent death. [4]
  • CBT can reduce death anxiety by addressing unhelpful beliefs and avoidance; seek individualized professional assessment when fear disrupts life. [2] [3] [4]
  • Any exposure work should be planned collaboratively with a trained clinician, using safe gradual steps rather than forced confrontation; normal medical care should be maintained. [4] [3]

Tokophobia — Severe Fear of Childbirth

A source-backed artistic explanation of tokophobia, its possible triggers and symptoms, avoidance and individualized maternity and mental-health support.

Research behind the infographic

  • Tokophobia is an established term for severe or phobic fear of childbirth, not ordinary uncertainty about birth. [1] [2]
  • Anxiety may occur even when someone wants a child; symptoms and experiences vary. [1]
  • Anticipatory anxiety can increase during pregnancy; thoughts about birth, negative birth accounts and memories of a traumatic previous birth may be associated with fear. [1]
  • Anxiety symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, disturbed sleep and panic symptoms. [1]
  • Avoidance can involve not talking or thinking about birth and avoiding antenatal education; isolation and feeling unsupported can also occur. [1]
  • Primary tokophobia can occur without prior experience of birth; secondary tokophobia can follow a difficult or traumatic birth. [1]
  • Fears may focus on harm to the parent or baby; maternity teams discuss birth options and develop plans that account for both physical and mental health. Fear alone does not measure individual obstetric risk. [1]
  • People with tokophobia should be offered discussion with a professional experienced in supporting this fear. [2]
  • Support can include speaking with a midwife or obstetrician, perinatal mental-health referral, psychological therapy such as CBT, and a collaborative birth plan including pain-relief and birth options. [1] [2]
  • Treatment is individualized to symptoms and the anxiety condition; education is not an individual diagnosis. [2] [3]
